analysis.one_liner: Declares federal civil rights law covers discrimination by private parties, including during contract performance.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee: introduced with 3 cosponsors, it received no hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written into law that federal civil rights protections (the equal-contract-rights statute, 42 U.S.C. 1981) apply against discrimination by private parties, not just government, and that those protections cover the entire life of a contract, not just signing or suing to enforce it. It came as a response to the Supreme Court's 1989 Patterson v. McLean Credit Union decision, which read that statute as not covering what happens after a contract is formed. The bill carried carve-outs: it would not apply to personal services between individuals outside business dealings, and it would not apply to employment at employers too small to be covered by Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (fewer than 15 employees). It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its civil rights subcommittee, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are refused a contract, or have the terms or performance of a contract cut back, because of who they are would gain a federal cause of action covering that conduct, closing the gap the Supreme Court opened in 1989. Workers at employers with 15 or more employees would keep a federal remedy for discrimination in hiring and in the terms of their jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People facing discrimination in private contracts

how_it_helps.text: The bill would declare that the equal-rights protections of section 1977 of the Revised Statutes (42 U.S.C. 1981) protect all persons against discrimination by private parties, not only by government.

It would extend those protections to the carrying out of a contract, affording the same protection during performance as in making or enforcing the contract, overruling the effect of the Supreme Court's 1989 Patterson decision for covered conduct.

Workers at employers meeting the Civil Rights Act of 1964 definition (15 or more employees) would keep the protections in employment relationships, and individuals would keep them in business-related dealings with other individuals.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and individuals accused of discriminating while performing contracts would face federal lawsuits, including damages claims. Small employers (under 15 employees) would be exempt from these employment claims, and private individuals hiring personal, non-business services would be exempt as well. Courts would absorb additional discrimination cases.

drawbacks.text: The bill would exempt employers with fewer than 15 employees from employment discrimination claims under section 1981, a carve-out that would actually narrow existing protections for workers at small businesses, since the statute itself has no size threshold.
It would also exempt individuals providing purely personal services not connected with their business, leaving discrimination in those transactions without this federal remedy.

The bill addressed only one of the 1989 Supreme Court rulings narrowing civil rights law; the broader civil rights coalition pursued more sweeping legislation (enacted in 1991) that this modest bill did not attempt to match, and businesses would still have faced new litigation costs in covered contract-performance disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a real but narrow fix: it would have restored federal protection against discrimination in the performance of private contracts, which the Supreme Court's 1989 Patterson decision had stripped away. Its employment carve-out for employers with fewer than 15 employees and its exemption for personal services between individuals would have left significant gaps, and it did not address the other 1989 rulings that weakened employment discrimination law. A supporter could honestly call it a partial repair; a critic could call it inadequate on one side and a source of new litigation on the other.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee sent it to its civil rights subcommittee, which never took it up, so it simply expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Courter introduced the Civil Rights Enforcement Act of 1989 on July 20, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Judiciary.
Five days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights, the standard step that moves a bill out of the full committee's hands.
No hearing, markup, or vote followed. The bill attracted only 3 cosponsors, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1991, with the bill still parked in subcommittee.
Congress eventually dealt with the same Supreme Court rulings more broadly in the Civil Rights Act of 1991, passed the following Congress; this bill played no role in that outcome.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses and individuals who would have faced federal discrimination claims over how they carry out contracts were spared that exposure because the bill died. People experiencing discrimination in contract performance gained nothing, and remained under the narrower protections left by the Supreme Court's 1989 rulings until the Civil Rights Act of 1991.

for.name: Rep. Jim Courter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 20, 1989, to extend federal civil rights protections to private discrimination and post-signing contract conduct.

against.name: House Committee on Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its civil rights subcommittee on July 25, 1989, and the full committee never acted on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Don Edwards
against.role: Chair, House Civil and Constitutional Rights Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the subcommittee that never took up the bill.

sides.party_line_note: There were no recorded votes; the sponsor and two of the three cosponsors were Republicans, with one Democrat, and the Democratic-led committee never moved the bill, so no partisan pattern was ever tested.

industries.industry: Businesses that contract with customers and vendors
industries.note: The bill would have exposed businesses to federal discrimination lawsuits over how they perform contracts, a new litigation risk in everyday commercial dealing. That cost is the mirror image of the protection the bill offered to people discriminated against.

The bill would have exempted small employers from employment claims under section 1981, insulating them from suits that the statute itself does not limit by firm size. Their workers would have had one fewer route to challenge discrimination.

industries.industry: Providers of personal services (domestic and household hiring)
industries.note: Individuals providing personal services not connected to their business would have been exempt, so discrimination in those transactions would carry no federal remedy under this law.
